```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("_setup.R")
# Read the sample sheet for the subset of the cohort used in this tutorial.
ss <- read.csv("data/sample_sheet.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ss <- ss[order(ss$slide, ss$array_pos), ]
```

## Overview

This tutorial is written for anyone new to array-based
DNA methylation analysis. The tutorial is primarily written using R, but instructions are provided such that 
those with little to no previous programming experience should be able to follow. It walks through quality control (QC) and 
preprocessing from raw Illumina IDAT files (or a partially processed methylation matrix), 
running an EWAS, and post-EWAS steps such as secondary analyses and annotation of results. This tutorial uses real,
publicly available data to showcase the critical decisions in pre-processing and modeling that occur due to data 
missingness, bias, or confounding that comes with real datasets. By the end, you should understand how to:

- read raw two-channel IDATs into R;
- run standard QC checks for methylation array data;
- normalize methylation data;
- identify which probes to filter prior to running an EWAS;
- create proxies for genetic ancestry or tobacco smoking;
- estimate blood cell composition;
- identify and correct for technical variation;
- fit an epigenome-wide model;
- run secondary regional analyses;
- add functional annotation to results

## The Grady Trauma Project (GTP)

This tutorial uses whole blood Illumina Methylation EPIC (v1, 850k probes) array data from the Grady Trauma Project
(GSE132203), accessed through NCBI's GEO database. This study is a case-control cohort of individuals with trauma 
and PTSD. In total, there are 795 individuals in the GTP cohort, although only a subset of 96 
individuals are used for the tutorial so everything can be run on a standard laptop.

The GTP was chosen for a number of reasons. First, it had raw IDATs deposited so we could show how to download and 
process from raw files. Second, because it has an unusually complete set of phenotype data for a publicly available 
dataset. Many public datasets deposited provide limited phenotype data. For the purposes of teaching, we wanted a dataset 
which did have many important variables deposited. This way, we are able to show how to estimate or 
create proxy variables when such data is not deposited, and provide comparisons to what was originally deposited to 
show evidence these methods are sound.

## The subset

The subset of 96 individuals used for the tutorial were selected from the full 795 balanced for PTSD case-control 
status and Sex. Below is a summary of the key characterstics of the 96-sample subset including PTSD status, sex, race
(self-reported), and mean age. We also show that the selected 95 do not have confounding of PTSD status with the 
technical variable 'Slide'. This type of confounding would make it impossible to distinguish if signals identified were due to true 
biological differences or technical artifacts.   

```{r}
#| label: subset-characteristic-summary
# Make a summary table of cohort characteristics
bal <- list(
  PTSD          = table(ss$ptsd, useNA = "ifany"),
  Sex           = table(ss$gender),
  Race          = table(ss$race, useNA = "ifany"))
bal
# Calculate and report age statistics
cat("\nAge: range", paste(range(ss$age, na.rm=TRUE), collapse="-"),
    "| mean", round(mean(ss$age, na.rm=TRUE), 1), "\n")
# Calculate and report if there is confounding of PTSD and Slide
cat("Chips carrying both PTSD classes:",
    sum(tapply(ss$ptsd, ss$slide, function(x) length(unique(na.omit(x)))>1)),
    "of", length(unique(ss$slide)), "\n")
```


## Table of Contents

Below is an overview of each Chapter of this tutorial and a brief description of what it covers:

- **[Background](background.qmd)** — what DNA methylation is and how arrays measure it. 
- **[0. Setup](00_setup.qmd)** — setting up software environments, downloading IDATs, assessing computational resources.
- **[1. Quality control](01_qc.qmd)** — detection p-values, intensity, predicted sex, SNP identity.
- **[2. Normalization](02_normalization.qmd)** — within- and between-array normalization.
- **[3. Probe filtering](03_probe_filtering.qmd)** — detection-p, cross-reactive, poor mapping, and ancestry-aware SNP masks.
- **[4. Cell composition](04_cell_composition.qmd)** — reference-based deconvolution, validated against deposited proportions.
- **[5. Genetic ancestry PCs](05_genetic_pcs.qmd)** — genetic ancestry principal components: what they are and how to estimate them. 
- **[6. Batch effects](06_batch_effects.qmd)** — technical variation correction; ComBat and surrogate variables.
- **[7. EWAS](07_ewas.qmd)** — association modeling with R.
- **[8. Snakemake pipeline](08_pipeline.qmd)** — **OPTIONAL** EWAS using a reproducible Snakemake workflow.
- **[9. Annotation](09_annotation.qmd)** — mapping top CpGs to genes, regions (DMRs), and adding functional annotation to results.

Each chapter's inputs are either available online to download or are created and saved from the previous chapter. There 
is a [Zenodo archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22135215) of all chapter inputs, intermediate files, and outputs so that you can check your work along the 
way or skip sections that you don't have the compute resources to perform yourself.
